verdict.reasoning: Patient states: "I've had a lot of pain in my lower tummy in the last two days. I feel kind of hot and sweaty."
When asked location: Doctor: "Is it in the middle or to one side?" Patient: "Not the middle, in the middle." indicating midline lower abdominal pain.
Patient: "No, I just a bit nausea but no vomiting." and later "just a bit of nausea but not vomiting."
Patient: "I had been constipated in like in the last last week, but now it's fine."
Doctor: "When did you last go to the toilet?" Patient: "Like two hours ago." followed by confirmation it was normal.
Patient: "there was some like slight blood in the urine, but like it was a little bit pink."
Doctor: "Are you having to go more often than normal?" Patient: "Yeah, a little bit, but I'm also drinking a lot in these days."
Doctor: "Any pain when you pass water?" Patient: "No, that's fine."
Doctor: "Are you more thirsty than normal?" Patient: "Yeah." and earlier notes drinking a lot: "I'm also drinking a lot in these days."
Patient: "Yes, I measured it, but it's fine. Like around 37." and "No, no, I just measured like one hour ago."
Doctor: "no similar problems to this before?" Patient: "No."
Doctor: "are you getting any pain higher up in your stomach?" Patient: "No, no, nothing of that."
Same exchange: Doctor: "Any acid coming up into your throat or anything like that?" Patient: "No, no, nothing of that."
Doctor: "And any other discharge below?" Patient: "No."
Doctor: "have you been abroad recently?" Patient: "No, no, no."
Doctor: "Have you had any other medical problems in the past?" Patient: "No, no, nothing… Like normal stuff like cold, flu." Doctor: "Nothing significant."
Doctor: "Do you take any regular medications?" Patient: "No."
Patient: "I've had just the implant, contraceptive implant. But like for one year now, no more." indicating it was removed about a year ago.
Doctor: "Any allergies to medications?" Patient: "Yes, amoxy." (amoxicillin).
Patient: "Actually my mom had breast cancer… it was then cured."
Doctor: "Who do you live with at home?" Patient: "With my parents."
Patient: "I drink alcohol. Let's say four times per week." and "a beer per time? Let's say average."
Doctor: "do you smoke or drink alcohol regularly?" Patient: "Yes." then clarifies "So I don't smoke, I drink alcohol."
Patient: "Yes, I measured it… Like around 37." and "I just measured like one hour ago."
Doctor: "it may be possible that you might be having an infection in the urine." This follows discussion of lower tummy pain, urinary frequency, and pink urine.
The transcript records alcohol intake (about four beers per week) but does not classify it as "moderate" or provide an assessment label of alcohol use.
Amoxicillin allergy is elicited: "Any allergies to medications?" / "Yes, amoxy." This is part of the clinical assessment.
Family history of breast cancer is explicitly discussed: "my mom had breast cancer… then cured," which is information taken into the assessment.

Doctor: "It may be possible that you might be having an infection in the urine… It might be worth taking a three day course of antibiotics" and "twice a day for three days." No specific antibiotic name is given.
Doctor: "if the pain is getting worse or you have a high temperature or back pain, or develop any new symptoms or you feel like it's not getting better, then we should speak to you again."
Doctor advises follow-up/face-to-face: "we might need to see you face to face for an examination" if pain worsens or no improvement, and also mentions contact again if recurrence.
Doctor: "Have you allocated a pharmacy with Babylon?" Patient: "Yes." and doctor plans to send prescription there.
There is no mention of monitoring or reviewing alcohol use in the plan; alcohol is only quantified in history.
The amoxicillin allergy is explicitly identified during the consultation ("Yes, amoxy"), which in context of an e-consult implies it is entered/documented in the chart.
Doctor: "if the pain is getting worse or you have a high temperature or back pain, or develop any new symptoms or you feel like it's not getting better, then we should speak to you again."
Doctor: "we might need to see you face to face for an examination" if pain worsens or there is no improvement/recurrence.
Nausea/vomiting review: "No, I just a bit nausea but no vomiting." and later "just a bit of nausea but not vomiting."
Doctor asks about higher stomach pain and patient denies: "are you getting any pain higher up in your stomach?" / "No, no, nothing of that."
Same ROS: "Any acid coming up into your throat or anything like that?" Patient: "No, no, nothing of that."
Doctor: "And any other discharge below?" Patient: "No." indicating no abnormal vaginal discharge.
